metadata.title: Trump withdraws Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, as his nominee to lead ICE

sources.news_title: The withdrawal leaves ICE without a Senate-confirmed director as acting chief David Venturella stays in place, and the agency has lacked one since 2017.
sources.text:
When it comes to the war in Iran, my supposition is that the economic negativity driving the country — and creating an environment where Democrats could do very well in the midterms — is entirely about one thing: the price of gas. The war is incredibly unpopular, but it’s different from the war in Iraq. Both were very expensive, but Iraq brought coffins back at a scale we haven’t seen here. The biggest difference is what Americans are paying at the pump.
According to AAA’s live average, gas is at $4.44 nationally. It’s higher in states like California and New York, but even here in Texas, where we have relatively low gas prices, it’s edging toward $4. During the memorandum of understanding, that son of a bitch kissed the twos. Before the war in Iran, it was sitting around the twos. It’s not good right now.
The question is whether this is Iran’s play. Iran is extraordinarily sophisticated in its understanding of the American electorate and the American democratic system. Are they timing their greatest chaos in the region to spike the price of oil as high as possible during election season? The United States appeared to have established a flow of tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, but now we’ve seen missiles and drones fired at American vessels and major damage to Saudi Arabia’s 745-mile east-west pipeline.
That pipeline can move four to five million barrels a day — roughly 4 to 5 percent of the global supply. Saudi Aramco has already told three European refiners they won’t receive their full September allotments, forcing them to buy emergency stock on the open market. Because oil is a globally traded commodity, that drives up the price. Chevron CEO Mike Wirth has warned that stockpile releases and access to previously restricted oil stored abroad had constrained prices, but those buffers are now played out. Iran has been warning about $200-a-barrel oil since the beginning of the conflict.
The obvious historical comparison is Jimmy Carter. But this isn’t 1979. Headline inflation was 11.8 percent then, compared with 3.4 percent now, and unemployment was 6 percent instead of 4.1 percent. We’re doing better by those measures, but will any of it matter? Gas was 98 cents a gallon in August 1979. In August 2026, it was $4.20, and it’s even higher now.
The sunniest version of Trump’s tariff policy was that he’d become the greatest energy president of all time and drive gas prices low enough to give him room to negotiate better trade deals. All of that went out the window with the rush into Iran. Even if you don’t totally hate the war from a foreign-policy standpoint, you can understand that this is political poison. It’s strychnine for the average voter. Electing Trump was, in part, a cry for economic relief from people who didn’t trust Joe Biden to provide it. The numbers currently suggest Democrats will receive that same benefit of the doubt. Whether it holds when people vote is the question.

The White House has withdrawn President Donald Trump’s nomination of former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer to lead US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), leaving the agency without a Senate-confirmed director.
The withdrawal was announced in a brief notice on Thursday, which did not give a reason for the decision. Schroyer’s nomination had stalled in the Senate after Republican Senator Rand Paul, who chairs the Homeland Security Committee, declined to advance it for a full vote.
Paul had sought more information from the White House about the fatal shootings of two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during separate confrontations involving federal immigration agents in Minneapolis in January.
Schroyer, who spent 29 years with the Oklahoma Highway Patrol and also served in the US Marines, was serving as a senior adviser to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin when Trump nominated him in June. Mullin, a former Oklahoma senator, is a close ally of Schroyer and oversees ICE through the Department of Homeland Security.
Trump had praised Schroyer at the time of his nomination, describing him as a “PATRIOT with real operational experience” and a “proven leader” with decades of law-enforcement experience.
However, Schroyer had limited experience specifically in immigration enforcement and had not previously led an agency the size of ICE.
ICE has not had a Senate-confirmed director since 2017 and has instead been led by acting chiefs. David Venturella is currently serving as acting director after Todd Lyons left the position in April.
The withdrawal means Venturella is expected to continue leading ICE while the administration considers its next nominee. The agency is central to Trump's immigration agenda and his push for a large-scale deportation programme.

The agency tasked with enforcing America’s immigration laws hasn’t had a Senate-confirmed director in eight years, and that streak will continue after the White House pulled President Trump’s nominee for the job on Thursday.
Richard Lance Shroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper tapped to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement, saw his confirmation bid collapse following a confrontation with Sen. Rand Paul during committee hearings. The Kentucky Republican, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, demanded details about investigations into agent-involved shootings in Minnesota before allowing the nomination to proceed.
The withdrawal marks a setback for the Trump administration’s border enforcement agenda at a time when ICE remains under acting leadership. The agency has operated without permanent, Senate-confirmed leadership since 2017, a remarkable stretch that spans multiple administrations and highlights the political minefield surrounding immigration enforcement.
Shroyer’s nomination appeared to face headwinds beyond the immediate dispute over shooting investigations. Paul has maintained a longstanding disagreement with Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, who previously served as a senator from Oklahoma. That friction between the libertarian-leaning Paul and the former Oklahoma lawmaker may have played a role in Shroyer’s failed confirmation attempt.
The connection between Shroyer and Mullin, both with Oklahoma ties, likely complicated the political calculus. Trump had nominated Shroyer to serve as assistant secretary at the Department of Homeland Security, the position that oversees ICE operations.
For an administration that has made immigration enforcement a cornerstone of its agenda, the lack of confirmed leadership at ICE creates challenges. Acting directors can implement policy, but Senate-confirmed leaders carry greater authority and permanence. They also send a signal of institutional stability to the thousands of agents and officers who carry out the difficult work of enforcing immigration law.
The Paul-Mullin dispute adds another layer of complexity to the confirmation process. Senate chairmen wield enormous power over nominations that come before their committees, and Paul has demonstrated a willingness to use procedural tools to press his concerns. His demand for information about agent-involved shootings suggests ongoing oversight tensions between Congress and the Department of Homeland Security.
The failed Shroyer nomination serves as a reminder that even within Republican ranks, confirmation battles can derail qualified nominees when senators have unresolved disputes with administration officials.

President Donald Trump has pulled the nomination of former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
The White House website identified Schroyer’s nomination as withdrawn on Thursday. Schroyer is a longtime personal friend of Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
Trump selected Schroyer for the post in late June, highlighting his 29 years in Oklahoma law enforcement and describing him as “a patriot with real operational experience.”
The White House did not immediately respond to Our News Outlet’s request for comment.
Schroyer’s nomination surprised many lawmakers, several of whom raised questions about whether he was qualified to run the federal immigration agency.
The Daily Mail reported in July that his confirmation was in jeopardy amid mounting questions about his experience and personal history, citing eight current and former DHS officials.
Court documents reviewed by Our News Outlet show that Schroyer’s second ex-wife accused him of going four years without paying child support for their two children.
Schroyer had never headed a law enforcement agency. Instead, he previously served as the head of Mullin’s security detail. After Mullin took over DHS following Kristi Noem’s ouster, he appointed Schroyer as a senior adviser at the department.
President Donald Trump withdrew Lance Schroyer’s nomination to become the next ICE director on Thursday
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had backed his Oklahoma friend, former state trooper Lance Schroyer, pictured above, for the ICE post, but Republicans pushed back against the nomination
The decision represents a significant setback for DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin because of his close personal ties to the former Oklahoma state trooper
Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul effectively stalled Schroyer’s nomination by seeking additional information from DHS about the federal officer-involved killings of two American citizens in Minneapolis earlier this year.
Reports have described Paul as one of the Republican lawmakers most skeptical of Schroyer’s qualifications.
As chairman, Paul controls the committee’s work, including the scheduling of confirmation hearings. No hearing was set for months.
The withdrawal is a major blow to Mullin, who oversees ICE in his role as DHS secretary and had a personal connection to Schroyer.
Schroyer is a veteran of the Oklahoma Highway Patrol. When Mullin was serving as a senator from the Sooner State, Schroyer worked as his security guard and unofficial chauffeur.
Within DHS, Mullin was reportedly mocked behind the scenes for promoting Schroyer despite the former trooper’s limited background in immigration matters.
Mullin, who replaced Noem as Homeland Security secretary in March, has said he spent two months conducting an extensive search for the right person to oversee ICE.
“I interviewed countless individuals, because we wanted someone not to just hold the position, someone that could also be confirmed, and here you have Lance that was literally right in front of me the whole time,” Mullin told Fox News this summer.
However, sources familiar with the search for an ICE director told Our News Outlet they had no knowledge of Mullin vetting other candidates.
Instead, sources say, Mullin tapped his ‘buddy’ and took his case directly to Trump without consulting two of the President’s top immigration advisers: Stephen Miller and Tom Homan.
Currently, David Venturella is serving as acting ICE director.
